editorNote: Big Blue puts a handle on the PC as the software business and public computer fairs grow into institutions.
morningLine: This week in 1984: IBM’s 30-pound portable arrives, the West Coast Computer Faire opens, and software takes center stage.

lead.headline: IBM Packs the PC Into a 30-Pound Portable
lead.dek: Big Blue answers the transportable-computer boom with a suitcase-sized machine that runs familiar PC software.
body: IBM announced the Portable Personal Computer 5155 Model 68 on February 29, bringing its own badge to a transportable category pioneered by Osborne and sharpened by Compaq. The new machine preserves IBM PC disk and software compatibility in a luggable case intended to move between desks.

Inside are an Intel 8088, 256K of memory, a nine-inch amber display and one 360K double-sided 5.25-inch diskette drive. The keyboard clips over the front for travel, while five expansion slots leave room for the familiar boards that have helped turn the PC into a business standard.

Portability remains a relative term. The 5155 weighs about 30 pounds, measures roughly 20 by 17 by 8 inches and requires an AC outlet. At $4,225 before a second drive or other options, it is built for professionals who value compatibility and mobility more than a light load.

The announcement confirms that transportable PCs are no passing novelty. IBM now expects customers to carry their software environment between offices, and rivals must answer a machine that combines the market leader’s name with the appeal of a computer that can travel.

stories.headline: West Coast Computer Faire Throws Open Its Doors
body: The ninth West Coast Computer Faire runs March 2-4 at San Francisco’s Civic Auditorium and Brooks Hall, gathering vendors, user groups and enthusiasts under one roof. Its show daily and proceedings range across software, floppy disks, communications and practical microcomputer applications.

The gathering remains part marketplace and part classroom. Timex/Sinclair clubs and other user communities stand beside commercial exhibitors, a reminder that personal computing is still being built jointly by manufacturers and people trading hard-won knowledge.

stories.headline: Software Becomes the Industry’s Main Event
body: Softcon in New Orleans drew a reported 14,600 visitors and 600 exhibitors to a show devoted entirely to software publishing. More than 12,000 packages were displayed as an industry once treated as an accessory to hardware asserted its own economic weight.

Industry estimates put 1984 software sales near $3.5 billion with growth of 40 to 50 percent a year. Lotus previewed Symphony, extending the 1-2-3 idea with fuller word processing, filing and communications, while publishers confronted development and launch costs that could reach millions.

stories.headline: PCjr Brings Better Games—and Awkward Compromises
body: IBM’s PCjr reaches reviewers with enhanced color graphics and sound, joystick support and instant-loading ROM cartridges. The $669 entry model carries 64K; the $1,269 enhanced version adds 128K and a 360K disk drive.

Its light system unit and gaming talents widen the PC family, but the infrared 62-key keyboard draws criticism and disk activity can swallow keystrokes. Reviewers see promise, yet cheaper dedicated game machines remain formidable rivals in the living room.
